articles.title: Como justificar o voto pelo e-Título? | G1
articles.standfirst: Justificativa para não votar pode ser feita pelo aplicativo e-Título ou diretamente em seções eleitorais.
articles.summary: Entenda o que é preciso levar para justificar o voto, quais documentos são aceitos e como fazer a justificativa eleitoral.
articles.body:
Aplicativo e-Título pode ser baixado pelos eleitores para acessar diversos serviços e encontrar o local de votação — Foto: Reprodução/Site do TSE

Não vai conseguir comparecer às urnas nas eleições de 2026? Você pode justificar a ausência sem sair de casa . O procedimento pode ser feito de forma totalmente digital pelos canais oficiais da Justiça Eleitoral, como o aplicativo e-Título e o Autoatendimento Eleitoral.

A justificativa é obrigatória para eleitores entre 18 e 70 anos que deixarem de votar em qualquer um dos turnos. Quem faltar aos dois turnos, se houver, precisa apresentar uma justificativa para cada ausência .

A justificativa pode ser feita no próprio dia da eleição ou, se isso não for possível, em até 60 dias após cada turno.

Como justificar o voto no dia da eleição pelo e-Título?

A forma mais simples é pelo aplicativo e-Título . O eleitor deve:

abrir o aplicativo e acessar a opção "Justificativa de ausência" ;

selecionar a eleição e o turno correspondente;

anexar documentos, se o sistema solicitar, como atestado médico ou comprovante de viagem;

guardar o código de acompanhamento para consultar posteriormente se a justificativa foi aceita.

Quem não conseguir fazer a justificativa no dia da votação ainda pode regularizar a situação em até 60 dias após cada turno . Veja as opções disponíveis:

Reprodução de tela do e-Título — Foto: Reprodução

preencha o formulário referente ao turno em que faltou;

anexe documentos que comprovem a impossibilidade de comparecer.

Reprodução de tela do TSE. — Foto: Reprodução/TSE

Pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral (no site do TSE)

Também é possível fazer o procedimento pelo sistema da Justiça Eleitoral. O eleitor deve:

selecionar a opção de justificativa eleitoral;

anexar documentos que comprovem o motivo da ausência.

Print do formulário de Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE). — Foto: Reprodução/TSE

Pelo formulário Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE)

Outra alternativa é enviar o Requerimento de Justificativa Eleitoral (RJE) à zona eleitoral. Nesse caso, é necessário:

anexar cópia dos documentos comprobatórios;

encaminhar o pedido à zona eleitoral responsável.

Eleitores com domicílio eleitoral no Brasil que estiverem fora do país no dia da votação também podem justificar a ausência. O pedido pode ser feito:

em até 30 dias após o retorno ao Brasil .

A justificativa pode ser apresentada por qualquer uma das três opções explicadas acima: pelo e-Título, pelo Autoatendimento Eleitoral ou pelo formulário RJE.

É importante anexar documentos que comprovem a viagem, como passagens, cartões de embarque ou carimbos no passaporte .

Já brasileiros inscritos na Zona Eleitoral do Exterior (ZZ) , que votam apenas para presidente da República, também têm até 60 dias após cada turno para apresentar a justificativa caso não compareçam à votação.

Quem deixa de votar e não apresenta justificativa fica sujeito ao pagamento de multa eleitoral, que pode custar até R$ 3,51.

Além disso, enquanto a situação não for regularizada, o eleitor pode enfrentar restrições para obter a certidão de quitação eleitoral, documento exigido em situações como posse em cargo público, inscrição em concursos públicos e emissão de passaporte.

Se a ausência ocorrer em três eleições consecutivas , sem justificativa e sem pagamento das multas, o título de eleitor poderá ser cancelado. Cada turno é considerado uma eleição para esse cálculo.

Candidatos ao governo do Ceará votam na manhã deste domingo (4) — Foto: Nayana Melo/Fabiane de Paula/SVM/Divulgação

Os candidatos do Ceará votaram neste domingo (4) em Fortaleza e em cidades da Região Metropolitana. Veja abaixo, em ordem alfabética, como foi a votação de cada um.

Ciro Gomes (PSDB) vota em Fortaleza. — Foto: Nayana Melo/ SVM

Ciro Gomes votou por volta das 10h50 na sede da Secretaria da Saúde do Ceará (Sesa), no bairro Praia de Iracema, em Fortaleza. Ele estava acompanhado do candidato a vice Roberto Cláudio e dos candidatos ao Senado pelo Ceará Capitão Wagner e Alcides Fernandes, dentre outros apoiadores.

"Eu chego extremamente esperançoso, embora com uma ponta de revolta, porque a ditadura corrupta que se instalou no Ceará, sob a coordenação do Camilo Santana, está fazendo de tudo para tomar essa eleição da liberdade do povo, que está em nossa direção claramente. [...] A gente sabe, mais ou menos, como pulsa o coração do povo do Ceará. Ontem [sábado, 3], em Sobral, chegou a ser para além de emocionante, chegou a ser comovente", disse.

Elmano vota em Caucaia, no Ceará. — Foto: Fabiane de Paula/Sistema Verdes Mares (SVM)

Elmano de Freitas votou por volta das 10h na Escola Francisco Martins de Morais, em Caucaia . Ele chegou ao local de votação por volta das 9h30, acompanhado do senador Camilo Santana, da candidata a vice Gabriella Aguiar, do prefeito de Fortaleza Evandro Leitão, da candidata ao Senado Luizianne Lins (Rede) e do candidato ao Senado Cid Gomes (PSB), dentre outros apoiadores.

"Nós estamos aqui na expectativa muito positiva de que no final do dia nós teremos uma apuração que vai, de fato, consolidar uma grande vitória desse projeto político. Aqui é um time, aqui a gente trabalha de maneira coletiva, todos juntos. A mensagem de esperança, uma mensagem de muita confiança, de que nós vamos poder fazer um estado que está avançando muito, sabendo que tem muita coisa para fazer", disse.

Vera Lúcia (Novo) vota em Fortaleza — Foto: Divulgação

Vera Lúcia votou por volta das 11h no Centro Pastoral Maria Mãe da Igreja, em Fortaleza. Ela chegou ao local de votação acompanhada de aliados políticos.

“O voto é a única forma de mudança. Espero que o Partido Novo cresça no Ceará. É um partido que tem valores inegociáveis, e provamos isso nessa campanha. Não negociamos o nosso voto”, afirmou.

articles.title: Fachin vota em Brasília: 'Eleições íntegras e auditáveis são o motor da democracia' | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do STF ficou cerca de 35 minutos na fila. Após votar, defendeu o exercício da soberania popular e disse que representantes eleitos e votos depositados nas urnas devem ser respeitados.
articles.summary: Presidente do STF ficou cerca de 35 minutos na fila. Após votar, defendeu o exercício da soberania popular e disse que representantes eleitos e votos depositados nas urnas devem ser respeitados.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) e do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ), Luiz Edson Fachin , votou em Brasília na manhã deste domingo (4).

Ele chegou ao Centro de Ensino Fundamental 214 Sul, na Asa Sul, por volta das 11h05 e ficou cerca de 35 minutos na fila antes de votar. Enquanto esperava, conversou com pessoas presentes.

O ministro estava acompanhado da esposa, Rosana Fachin, que votou primeiro. Fachin votou na sequência, por volta das 11h45.

“Eleições periódicas, íntegras, seguras, transparentes e auditáveis são o motor da democracia”, afirmou Fachin após votar.

Fachin aguardando para votar na Asa Sul. — Foto: Alexandro Martello/g1

Fachin disse que as eleições são uma fonte de legitimidade dos representantes escolhidos pelo voto e classificou o dia de votação como um exercício da soberania popular.

Ele parabenizou a Justiça Eleitoral e a sociedade brasileira pelo “exercício de cidadania”.

O presidente do STF também afirmou que o voto representa um exercício de liberdade e uma escolha sobre o futuro do país.

Segundo ele, o processo democrático representa uma aposta na capacidade do Brasil de superar obstáculos e encontrar soluções em áreas como saúde, educação, infraestrutura e segurança pública.

“É importante que toda cidadã e todo cidadão exerça seu direito de votar”, afirmou.

Ministro Edson Fachin aguarda na fila antes de votar na Asa Sul. — Foto: Alexandro Martello/g1

Fachin também defendeu o respeito ao resultado das urnas, aos representantes escolhidos pelos eleitores e a cada voto.

“[Que] saibamos, concluída a votação, quem serão os nossos representantes, que merecem o nosso respeito, bem como merece o nosso integral respeito o voto que tenha sido depositado na urna”, disse.

articles.title: Jaques Wagner vota em Salvador nas eleições para o Senado | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao Senado votou na Superintendência Federal de Agricultura (SFA), no bairro dos Aflitos.
articles.summary: Jaques Wagner vota em Salvador na Superintendência Federal de Agricultura e antecipa participação em comitiva com Jerônimo Rodrigues e Rui Costa.
articles.body:
Jaques Wagner votou neste domingo — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O candidato ao Senado, Jaques Wagner ( PT ), votou neste domingo (4), na Superintendência Federal de Agricultura (SFA), no bairro dos Aflitos, em Salvador .

Inicialmente, a equipe do candidato à reeleição do governo da Bahia, Jerônimo Rodrigues (PT), informou que Jaques Wagner faria parte de uma comitiva que também contaria com a presença do também candidato ao Senado, Rui Costa (PT).

No entanto, Jaques Wagner votou sozinho, antes de Jerônimo e Rui Costa. O motivo da antecipação do voto não foi divulgado.

Jaques Wagner nasceu no Rio de Janeiro, mas fez carreira política na Bahia, onde ocupou cargos de deputado federal e governador.

Sua iniciação na vida política teve origem no movimento estudantil, a partir de 1968. Seu primeiro cargo eletivo foi em 1990, como deputado federal. Foi reeleito duas vezes (em 1994 e em 1998).

Wagner também ocupou o Ministério do Trabalho no governo Lula (entre janeiro de 2003 e janeiro de 2004) e foi ministro da Secretaria Especial do Conselho de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social. Com a crise do "mensalão", em 2005, foi designado Ministro das Relações Institucionais.

Em 2006, Wagner foi eleito governador da Bahia. Ele cumpriu dois mandatos no cargo, entre os anos de 2007 e 2014.

Quando foi eleito governador pela primeira vez, em 2006, Jaques Wagner quebrou um ciclo de quatro mandatos consecutivos do Partido da Frente Liberal (PFL) à frente da Bahia. Ele chegou ao poder depois de derrotar seu principal concorrente na disputa, o então governador Paulo Souto (PFL), lançado à política pelo senador Antônio Carlos Magalhães (PFL) e que o havia derrotado quatro anos antes.

Jaques Wagner também foi ministro da Defesa entre janeiro e outubro de 2015 e, em seguida, assumiu a Casa Civil, cargo que ocupou até março de 2016, no segundo mandato da presidente Dilma Rousseff. Ele também chegou a ser Ministro-Chefe do Gabinete Pessoal da Presidência em 2016.

articles.title: Presidente do TRE-MG diz que vai apurar uso de celular por Zema | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do TRE-MG afirmou que o caso será apurado e lembrou que o uso de celular na cabine de votação é proibido. Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, a violação do sigilo do voto é crime previsto no Código Eleitoral, mas eventual punição depende de denúncia formal do Ministério Público.
articles.summary: Segundo a Justiça Eleitoral, a violação do sigilo do voto é crime previsto no Código Eleitoral, mas eventual punição depende de denúncia formal do Ministério Público.
articles.body:
O presidente do TRE-MG, Carlos Henrique Perpétuo Braga, afirmou neste domingo (4) que a Justiça Eleitoral vai apurar o uso de celular pelo candidato à Presidência Romeu Zema dentro da cabine de votação, em Araxá ( veja vídeo acima ).

Segundo o magistrado, o uso do aparelho no momento do voto é proibido, e a violação do sigilo da votação pode configurar crime eleitoral. O presidente ressaltou, porém, que eventual responsabilização depende de uma denúncia formal apresentada pelo Ministério Público.

"Em primeiro lugar, valem as regras, e as regras dizem que não é possível usar o celular na cabine de votação. Nós temos que apurar especificamente o caso, verificar os seus contornos para emitir uma opinião, um veredito, uma decisão final. Isso é irregular e caracteriza crime. Isso pode, inclusive, gerar pena de detenção", disse o presidente do TRE-MG.

A fala do presidente foi durante uma coletiva do TRE-MG, em Belo Horizonte , ao apresentar um balanço parcial sobre as eleições no estado.

O g1 entrou em contato com o Ministério Público de Minas Gerais e aguarda retorno.

Questionado sobre o uso do celular dentro da cabine de votação, Romeu Zema afirmou que entrou no local com o aparelho por hábito e disse que não foi alertado previamente.

"Eu ando com o celular o dia todo. Ele é quase como se fosse um dedo. Ninguém me lembrou ali e eu fui votar normalmente. Não fotografei nada, não fiz nada com o celular ali. Fui só votar mesmo. A cola eu levei no papel", afirmou Zema.

Segundo a assessoria de Romeu Zema, após votar, ele foi até a casa dos pais, próxima ao local de votação, antes de retornar para Belo Horizonte.

Momento em que o candidato à presidência da República, Romeu Zema, vai para cabine de votação com celular nas mãos. — Foto: GloboNews

articles.title: Diretor da PF diz que não há riscos para embaixadas e consulados: 'Não encontramos elementos' | G1
articles.standfirst: Embaixadas estrangeiras no Brasil emitiram alertas de segurança nesta sexta-feira (2) e citaram as eleições como um dos motivos para recomendar cautela a cidadãos que estão no país.
articles.summary: Embaixadas estrangeiras no Brasil emitiram alertas de segurança nesta sexta-feira (2) e citaram as eleições como um dos motivos para recomendar cautela a cidadãos que estão no país.
articles.body:
O diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, afirmou neste domingo (4) que investigações não identificaram possibilidade de risco ou indícios de planos de ataque contra embaixadas em Brasília.

A PF cumpriu dois mandados de busca e apreensão na sexta-feira (2) em uma investigação sobre um suposto plano contra a Embaixada dos Estados Unidos no Brasil. Os investigadores miraram dois suspeitos.

A ação ocorreu após representações diplomáticas estrangeiras no Brasil emitirem alertas de segurança na sexta-feira (2). As embaixadas citaram as eleições como um dos motivos para recomendar cautela a cidadãos que estão no país.

"Não encontramos elementos concretos sobre a existência de risco para nenhuma embaixada. Não havia plano, não havia nada que tenhamos identificado", afirmou Andrei Rodrigues.

Embaixada dos Estados Unidos, em Brasília — Foto: TV Globo/Reprodução

Estados Unidos e Austrália chegaram a suspender o atendimento presencial em representações diplomáticas por questões de segurança.

O governo dos EUA não deixou claro que tipo de serviços consulares fornecidos pela embaixada foram suspensos. Também não especificou se seguirá emitindo vistos e passaportes no período.

A TV Globo apurou que os dois alvos foram identificados depois postarem comentários em plataformas e redes sociais.

A princípio, os suspeitos não têm ligação, mas isso ainda é investigado. Segundo fontes, postagens como as identificadas são frequentes nas redes sociais.

A GloboNews apurou que governo americano avisou sobre as suspeitas à Embaixada dos EUA, que comunicou ao Ministério das Relações Exteriores, que, por sua vez, acionou a PF.

O Canadá não fechou as portas da embaixada, mas recomendou que cidadãos tenham cautela no Brasil e citou as eleições no país.

Assim como a Irlanda, que orientou cidadãos no Brasil a manter "alto grau de cautela". O governo irlandês informou as datas dos dois turnos das eleições e alertou para a possibilidade de manifestações políticas.

O Reino Unido emitiu um alerta semelhante em 29 de setembro. Segundo o governo britânico, manifestações podem ocorrer pelo Brasil sem aviso prévio, e a situação pode mudar rapidamente.

A Alemanha também divulgou um alerta antes do anúncio dos Estados Unidos de quinta-feira (1º). O comunicado cita a possibilidade de manifestações e confrontos.

articles.standfirst: Com atualização em tempo real dos 26 estados e do Distrito Federal, a página do g1 vai acompanhar a apuração das urnas em todo o país. A home do portal também terá novas funcionalidades para facilitar o acompanhamento dos resultados.
articles.summary: Com atualização em tempo real dos 26 estados e do Distrito Federal, a página do g1 vai acompanhar a apuração das urnas em todo o país. A home do portal também terá novas funcionalidades para facilitar o acompanhamento dos resultados.
articles.body:
Eleições 2026: apuração em tempo real — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Acompanhe a apuração das eleições 2026 no domingo, 4 de outubro, ao vivo, pelo g1 . Ao todo, os 26 estados e o Distrito Federal elegerão governadores, senadores, deputados federais e deputados estaduais e distritais, além da votação para Presidente da República.

Os dados são do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) .

Na página de apuração do g1 , o usuário pode acessar os números de votos em cada unidade federativa em tempo real e acompanhar a apuração.

Além das páginas de apuração, o g1 terá uma série de recursos especiais para facilitar o acompanhamento das Eleições 2026. Resultados em tempo real, vídeo ao vivo, mapas interativos e conteúdos automatizados estarão disponíveis nas homes e em páginas especiais do portal (veja abaixo).

Além da apuração nacional, acesse diretamente a página de apuração dos estados e DF:

O que você encontra na página de apuração

Ao acessar o estado desejado, você encontrará um resumo da corrida eleitoral presidencial ou do estado, começando pela lista dos candidatos .

Até as 17h de domingo (4), os candidatos estarão listados por ordem alfabética. Conforme os dados da apuração forem liberados pelo TSE, os nomes serão listados de acordo com a quantidade de votos recebidos.

Em seguida, um gráfico mostrará, do início ao fim da apuração, a evolução dos candidatos mais bem colocados ( imagem abaixo ).

Será possível navegar pelos mapas interativos do Brasil e dos estados para ver os resultados da eleição para presidente e governador nos 5.571 municípios.

Em 108 cidades e no Distrito Federal, a consulta será ainda mais detalhada: além do resultado por zona eleitoral e local de votação, o eleitor poderá conferir os votos de sua própria urna.

Página de apuração tem link para mapa com números locais — Foto: Reprodução

Mapa de Minas Gerais na página de apuração — Foto: g1

Ao navegar pela tela ou ao escolher a opção de deputados federais, estaduais e senadores, no menu superior da página de apuração, você encontra não só os candidatos ao posto, mas também os votos em tempo real e a quantidade de cadeiras disponíveis.

Com 100% das urnas apuradas, a página vai trazer a sinalização dos eleitos para o Senado, a Câmara dos Deputados e as Assembleias Legislativas.

Cadeiras de Senadores e Deputados Federais — Foto: Reprodução/g1

Outras funcionalidades no g1 nas Eleições 2026

Além das páginas de apuração, o g1 terá novas funcionalidades nas Eleições 2026 para facilitar o acompanhamento dos resultados pelos eleitores.

Ao acessar o g1 , o leitor encontrará uma régua de apuração com os candidatos mais bem colocados e a atualização dos resultados em tempo real.

A funcionalidade estará disponível na home principal do g1 e nas páginas de Política e de Eleições das afiliadas do g1 em todo o Brasil, a partir das 7h do domingo (4).

As homes do g1, de Política e das afiliadas também terão um vídeo ao vivo com a cobertura nacional da TV e as principais informações sobre a apuração em todo o Brasil. A transmissão estará disponível a partir das 14h de domingo (4).

As homes do g1 , das afiliadas e suas páginas de Eleições também terão um mapa com a apuração em todo o Brasil. A experiência será a mesma disponível na home principal do g1 , com uma visão nacional dos resultados. O mapa ficará logo abaixo da manchete.

A cobertura especial das Eleições 2026 no g1 também terá uma página com mapas interativos, que permitirão aos eleitores navegar por todas as regiões do Brasil e acompanhar os resultados da votação em cada localidade.

Exemplo do mapa de apuração — Foto: Reprodução/g1

Textos automatizados e ferramentas exclusivas

A cobertura das Eleições 2026 no g1 também contará com uma série de conteúdos produzidos de forma automatizada, com ajuda de inteligência artificial e sob a supervisão de jornalistas.

Os textos vão permitir ao eleitor consultar candidatos e resultados da votação com diferentes níveis de detalhamento:

Quem são os candidatos : ferramenta com informações sobre os candidatos que disputam as eleições;

Candidatos eleitos : uma matéria para cada deputado federal, estadual e distrital eleito, publicada após a apuração de 100% das urnas;

Cidades por estado : página que reúne os municípios de cada estado e permite acessar informações sobre as cidades e, em seguida, os locais de votação;

Resultados por cidade: página que reúne os municípios de cada estado para consulta dos resultados da votação;

Como foi a votação por cidade: conteúdo publicado assim que a votação for concluída no município;

Como foi a votação por local de votação: detalhamento dos votos por urna e por local de votação, disponível assim que a votação for concluída na cidade.

articles.summary: Candidato ao Senado votou neste domingo (4) em Cruzeiro do Sul. Ele estava acompanhado de apoiadores e destacou a importância da democracia.
articles.body:
O candidato ao Senado pelo Acre Gladson Camelí (PP) votou neste domingo (4) na Escola Hugo Carneiro, em Cruzeiro do Sul , interior do Acre. Ele chegou ao local após às 9h.

Acompanhado da governadora Mailza Assis, da candidata a vice-governadora, Jéssica Sales, de assessores e apoiadores, conversou com eleitores na fila e votou minutos depois. Ao deixar o local de votação, falou com a imprensa e destacou como a democracia é fundamental no país. "

"A democracia é fundamental em todos os países. Então, agradecer, caminhando, conversando e agora chegou a hora do eleitor decidir quem será seus próximos representantes. E eu cumpro o meu papel como sempre. Tá aqui em Cruzeiro do Sul. Votando, fazendo meu papel de direito. Depois da eleição, descer do palanque e colocar em prática tudo que falamos em campanha", destacou.

Este ano, os eleitores do estado votam duas vezes para o Senado elegem dois senadores. Os dois mais votados, independente do percentual, vencem. Não é permitido votar duas vezes no mesmo candidato, caso contrário o segundo voto no mesmo nome será anulado.

Gladson Camelí, candidato ao Senado — Foto: Naiane Santos/Rede Amazônica Acre

Segundo o TSE, poderão votar 614.375 pessoas , um número 4,41% superior ao de 2022, que foi 588.433 . Os dados levam em conta a declaração dos eleitores sobre seu gênero ao se inscrever ou atualizar o cadastro na Justiça Eleitoral.

Ainda segundo o balanço, a capital do estado, Rio Branco , continua como a cidade com o maior eleitorado, com 270.350 eleitores, seguida de Cruzeiro do Sul, com 64.167 pessoas aptas a votar, e Sena Madureira , com 30.905 eleitores.

As informações apresentadas são usadas pela Justiça Eleitoral para organizar a eleição – por exemplo, para a distribuição das urnas e das equipes que vão atuar no dia da votação.

No estado, o Tribunal Regional Eleitoral do Acre (TRE-AC) conta com 2.270 seções eleitorais .

Quem não comparecer ao local de votação precisa justificar a ausência. O prazo para justificar é até 60 dias depois da votação.

Qual é a ordem de votação na urna eletrônica?

No primeiro turno, o eleitor fará seis escolhas, seguindo esta ordem:

Presidente da República, com dois dígitos.

Antes de confirmar cada voto, é importante conferir o nome, o número, a fotografia e os demais dados exibidos na tela.

Atenção especial para as duas vagas do Senado: é necessário escolher candidatos diferentes. Se o eleitor votar duas vezes no mesmo candidato, o segundo voto será anulado .

No dia da eleição, o eleitor pode votar vestindo uma bermuda, calçando chinelos ou com qualquer outra roupa que preferir.

articles.title: Trump, campaigning in Ohio, says the midterms will bring a ‘big surprise’
articles.summary: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will...
articles.body:
VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio's competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.

"I think we're going to have a big surprise, because they don't know what's happening," Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton.

"Just get out and vote," Trump added. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big. And we're going to shove it up their ass."

The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting Sen. Jon Husted and GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy.

Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio.

Husted's bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted's past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race.

The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group's investment in the state to $93 million.

"Sen. Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time," Trump said before relating conversations he's had with Thune and others: "They think he's phenomenal."

The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later.

In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war with Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he's not on the ballot.

"As a lifelong Republican who's voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we're going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter," Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio's Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. "I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls."

Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he's been making on the campaign trail this fall.

"When I run, we win," Trump said. "But for some reason, when I don't run, they draw 44% less people. So what I'm going to do is ask you to just pretend that I'm running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you're going to win, and we're going to win big."

Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race.

"Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we'll win," Husted said.

Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was "hugely important" in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters.

"We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we'll win every race," Triantafilou said in an interview. "Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump."

The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted's on the University of Dayton football team.

"Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend," an animated Gruden told the audience. "He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody."

Trump marveled about Husted's football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden.

"Nobody told me you were a great athlete," Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: "And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can't tie his shoes."

For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted's support for the Iran war to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally.

"Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he's only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests," Brown said in a statement from his campaign.

Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state's health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices are top of mind for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy's appeal, especially in rural parts of the state.

Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination.

"He was a nasty guy," Trump said of Ramaswamy. "But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He's actually got a great heart."

Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump's remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted's Ratepayer Protection Act , which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers.

Republicans, Trump said, are "taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities."

Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted.

"We want them," Trump said. "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China."

Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song "The Snake" — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory for trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio.

The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets.

At another point, the crowd broke into chants of "four more years" for the term-limited president.

"I'd love to do the four-more-year thing," Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks.

"We're driving them totally crazy," Trump said, referring to the media. "But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do."

articles.title: In crude Ohio rally speech, Trump says he may not help if Democrats win
articles.summary: VANDALIA, Ohio, Oct 3 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump used an Ohio rally on Saturday to mix profane attacks on Democrats with promises of financial hel...
articles.body:
VANDALIA, Ohio, Oct 3 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump used an Ohio rally on Saturday to mix profane attacks on Democrats with promises of financial help if Republicans win the midterms and a warning that he would be less willing to work with the state if Democrats prevail.

"Just get out ‌and vote," Trump said at a rally for Republican candidates, including US Senator Jon Husted and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. "If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to ‌win big, and we're going to shove it up their ass."

Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds in the November 3 elections, with Trump's popularity falling in recent months as higher prices persist for gasoline and other staples ​amid the US-Israeli war with Iran. Both Husted and Ramaswamy are in competitive races against Democratic opponents.

Former US Senator Sherrod Brown is running against Husted. Amy Acton is facing Ramaswamy.

Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, which will decide control of the narrowly divided House of Representatives and Senate, but Trump said Republicans would do better than critics expect. "I think we're going to have a big surprise because they don't know what's happening," he told the crowd in Vandalia, Ohio.

Ohio's is among eight US Senate races rated competitive. The state has turned into a campaign battlefield over data centers ‌and culture war issues such as youth transgender surgeries.

Trump repeatedly attacked ⁠Democrats during his speech, at one point calling them "dumb son of a bitches," while arguing that maintaining Republican control would give Ohio officials a direct line to his administration and make it easier for the state to secure federal help.

He said Ohio's elected Republican officials frequently call him seeking money for the ⁠state, adding that he would be less inclined to accommodate Democrats if they win key races. Referring to Acton, Trump said: "But I'm not going to help her."

Husted is counting on Trump to motivate supporters who might otherwise skip the midterms, but the senator also directly criticized Brown, a veteran Democrat, as someone who has accomplished little in his political career. "He's been in office for 50 years — can you name one thing that he has done ​for ​you?" Husted said at the rally.

A spokesperson for Brown's campaign criticized Husted for backing Trump's policy on Iran and ​said Husted supported "sweetheart tax deals" that lured data centers to Ohio.

"Jon Husted puts ‌corporations and billionaires first every time, and we all pay for it," Brown spokesperson Lauren Chou said in an email to Reuters.

Trump garnered more than 55% of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.

Ohio gasoline prices increased 35% over the past year to $4.16 per gallon on average, according to AAA, which compiles data on automobile travel. Trump's trade policy with Canada has led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3 billion worth of Ohio exports, based on 2025 figures, according to a CBC report.

Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday's rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war "on our terms" and in the interim, he is "showing people that I'm fighting for lower prices."

He spoke to a sympathetic crowd at the ‌rally, but he also needs to sell his message to people like independent voter Jonathan Smith.

Smith, a 19-year-old ​construction worker, held a sign reading, "Where are my lower gas prices?" outside his former high school in Vandalia, north of ​Dayton.

"I've got a wedding to save up for, and with gas prices continuously going up, ​it's getting harder and harder to put aside money," said Smith, adding he is still deciding whom to vote for in the Senate race.

Outside political groups ‌have poured tens of millions of dollars into Ohio, making Husted-Brown the second-most-expensive Senate ​race in the country, according to Federal Election Commission ​filings.

Rallygoers shared mixed opinions on the hot-button issue of data centers in the state.

"I'm not huge on the AI data centers," Samuel Clevenger, 20, said when discussing Husted's candidacy. But the apprentice plumber said he was encouraged to vote by Trump's attention to the state, as well as his 2025 policy capping taxes on overtime.

On the other side of the ​rally venue, Brenda White, 60, held a sign encouraging building in her ‌northeastern Ohio town: "DATA CENTER SOUTH LORAIN."

As Husted met voters in the bleachers, she urged the senator to support the center's construction in place of a steel mill. "You want ​a data center there?" Husted asked.

Before White posed for her photo with Husted, a man in the senator's entourage asked: "Can we do it without the sign?"

(Reporting by Bo ​Erickson and Nandita Bose; Editing by Sergio Non, Muralikumar Anantharaman, Rod Nickel, Deepa Babington and William Mallard)

articles.summary: "Hace falta más, muchísima más, vivienda pública", afirma el ministro de Transportes
articles.body: Óscar Puente, ministro de Transportes, ha analizado la crisis de la vivienda. El Partido Popular, entre otros actores, ha señalado que la mejor fórmula para subsanar este déficit es construir más inmuebles. El dirigente socialista se ha mostrado, en redes sociales, totalmente contrario a este planteamiento: "Que se plantee de nuevo que la solución al problema de precios de acceso a una vivienda (sea en renta o en propiedad) pasa por construir un millón de viviendas, solo es posible gracias a la confianza de la derecha en la desmemoria del pueblo". El titular de Transportes ha recordado, para justificar su razonamiento, el boom inmobiliario. "A principios de siglo, con el boom inmobiliario y la liberalización total del suelo, se llegó a construir al ritmo de 500.000 viviendas al año y los precios de la vivienda se duplicaron. Entre 2000 y 2008 se construyeron más de 4,5 millones de viviendas", ha indicado. "No había entonces "inmigrantes acaparándolas" (causa que invoca VOX) y sin embargo los precios no bajaron", ha añadido. Óscar Puente ha insistido en que la solución a la crisis inmobiliaria, según su criterio, no pasa por incrementar la cantidad de pisos y casas disponibles. "De nada sirve construir vivienda a mansalva si esta acaba en unas pocas manos, que es lo que sucedería con certeza si se aplicara esa solución. Y es que no hace falta más vivienda. Hace falta más, muchísima más, vivienda pública que presione los precios a la baja y facilite que las economías más débiles puedan acceder a ella", ha reflexionado. La crisis de la vivienda marca la agenda de la política española, generando numerosas movilizaciones sociales en todo el país. El pasado viernes, el Congreso de los Diputados no aprobó los dos decretos planteados por el Gobierno, abriendo un escenario político incierto. De hecho, el presidente Pedro Sánchez está valorando si adelanta las elecciones generales.

articles.title: Supreme Court kicks off new term with fresh questions over its legitimacy and its future
articles.summary: The Supreme Court opens its new term with major cases on gun rights, voter citizenship and religious liberty amid record-low public approval ratings.
articles.body: The Supreme Court begins its new term Monday, with renewed public and political concern over their recent rulings, the justices' personal safety and even their future makeup. Chief Justice John Roberts, surrounded by his eight colleagues, will call the court into public session precisely at 10 a.m. EDT with a pair of scheduled oral arguments. Their first case from the bench will be a major one: a federal-state environmental dispute over holding oil and gas companies liable for climate change harms. Other high-profile appeals are already on the argument docket: NEWSOM PROMISES NEW LEGAL FIGHT AFTER TRUMP GETS SUPREME COURT VICTORY ON MAIL-IN VOTING But the Supreme Court under Roberts' leadership continues to struggle against negative public attitudes over their reputation as a non-political actor upholding the law and Constitution. "The chief justice is in a tough position in that he is an institutionalist and a traditionalist at a time in our nation's history where a lot of institutions and traditions have come under pressure like they haven't in a long time," said Thomas Dupree, a leading appellate attorney and former top Justice Department official. "And so in many ways, he is trying to kind of buck a lot of the tide right now by really insisting and hewing to these traditions of the institutions that have governed Washington for a long time." Trump on the docket The new term will feature more constitutional disputes over the power of the executive, with current or anticipated fights over immigration, federal bureaucracy reforms and possibly the White House ballroom and Kennedy Center construction projects. And if recent history is any predictor, the justices are likely to offer a mixed, nuanced series of rulings both for and against President Donald Trump's ambitious agenda. The last term saw him and his allies lose over sweeping reciprocal tariffs, birthright citizenship and removal of Federal Reserve governors; but prevail on various immigration policies, mid-decade redistricting and political gerrymandering, and federal campaign spending. For the most part, the 6-3 conservative majority has greenlighted the administration's power, especially in a series of preliminary decisions from its so-called "shadow docket" that allow Trump to move ahead – for now – on a range of issues. The Trump Justice Department has won over 70% of its emergency cases before the Supreme Court since 2025 – applications that ask a challenged executive policy be enforced temporarily, while the larger issues are further litigated in the lower courts. Those included new federal rules for verifying a voter's citizenship status ahead of the November midterms; and approval for continued construction of the ballroom. Court legitimacy and public perception Decisions in Trump's second term have him and Republican lawmakers sharply criticizing their judicial losses on one hand, and Democratic leaders sounding the alarm when their side does not prevail. The judiciary has always weathered such criticism, but the personal tone of the attacks has only increased, as have the calls for sweeping accountability. Those on the right have demanded impeaching federal judges who block White House policies, while those on the left have renewed calls for drastic changes to the court's structure. The president himself amped up the tensions dramatically, after losing a key decision over federal efforts to restrict mail ballots for the midterm elections. In a wild Truth Social post, he took aim at the three members he appointed to the bench – Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," wrote Trump after the Sept. 14 ruling, adding, "The Court’s inability and unwillingness to do the right thing for our Country will go down, in a very negative way, in the annals of History." Those on the left have their own beefs. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told the National Association of Black Journalists that "dramatic Supreme Court reform is necessary... there's a variety of different options that are on the table and I think that we can't foreclose any single one of them." As the midterms approach, angry and energized Democrats hoping to take control of the House and maybe the Senate have tried to rally the base during the midterm races. Among their proposals are renewed calls for 18-year term limits for the justices, expanding the number on the bench to 13 or more from the current nine, and an independently enforced code of ethics. All this has added to increasing public perception the high court is motivated by something other than its constitutional obligations. A Washington Post/Ipsos poll in July found 46% of Americans think the justices rule on Trump administration policies based on their political views, while just 25% see the court as ruling based on the law. Gallup's July poll showed the Supreme Court's job approval slumped to a record low of 33% and a record high 61% disapproval, driven by a steep drop in Republicans' backing of the court since last year. And the most-recent Fox News survey revealed a 38% public job approval for the court, and a record high 45% believing the justices are too conservative. That was up from 34% in 2022, and a low of 16% in 2015 and 2010. Safety matters Numbers aside, the amplified partisan rhetoric is having real-world consequences. Several federal judges have told Fox News that budget shortfalls have compromised their physical security, at a time when they say threats against members of the bench have become more concerning. The U.S. Marshals report 370 threats made to federal judges as of July 1, a 31% year-over-year increase. "Extraordinary safety measures" have been taken in some cases by federal law enforcement, one federal judge told Fox News, without offering details. While "criticism is fair game, intimidation is a different thing entirely," Justice Elena Kagan told a congressional panel in July. "When political figures of any stripe are trying to intimidate judges and justices to do things that they like rather than the things that they don't, that's where we really have crossed a line." Justice Barrett told the same House committee, "The threat level is really high." On at least one occasion, she has had to wear a bulletproof vest away from the court, and was a victim of a swatting incident over the summer at her home. TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT Roberts' rules The job of managing the court's docket falls to Roberts, who has faced bipartisan criticism for perceived partisanship. Appointed by a Republican president, he more than any conservative on this current bench has been willing to rule against Trump and his Republican supporters. That mixed record has been especially acute in recent days, where his influence was apparent in a series of decisions on midterm election matters, separately favoring both political parties. That includes fights over congressional redistricting, mail ballots, a DHS database for voter eligibility and campaign ad spending. More such emergency disputes are expected to reach the high court in coming weeks, pre- and post-election. His colleagues have come to the chief justice's defense. "I don't see this as a court that is just like: We're just going to rubber stamp what the current administration does. You know, quite the opposite," Kagan said at a judicial conference in July. "I think that that is a bad rap." Roberts himself in May defended the court against accusations of partisanship. "We’re not simply part of the political process, and there's a reason for that, and I'm not sure that people grasp that as much as is appropriate," he said at a judicial conference. Looking ahead The court's new term will continue to be defined by various Trump executive actions being challenged by progressive states and private groups. That includes pending appeals over transgenders in the military, tariffs, private data access and federal agency cuts. Other upcoming challenges include mandated Ten Commandments displays in public schools, free speech fights and abortion access. Much of what the court decides to tackle will likely turn on whether Democrats can gain control Congress after November, and their ability to legislatively tame Trump's aggressive assertion of presidential power. "This term is once again, set to deliver us a series of decisions concerning some of the most fundamental aspects of our government, including the relationship among the three branches of our federal government, and the relationships between the federal government and the states," said legal analyst Dupree. "I think we're also going to see in the near future a lot of election-related cases about the right to vote, how you protect it, and how we ensure the integrity of our election. So this is a term that promises a lot of big decisions and frankly, something for everyone." TRUMP BLASTS SUPREME COURT 'DISASTER' AFTER JUSTICES RULE AGAINST HIM ON MAIL-IN VOTING Add to that the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy in coming months, with much of the speculation centered on 76-year-old Justice Samuel Alito. Fox News was the first to report earlier this spring he would stay on for another term that effectively ends in late June, and he plans to be on the bench Monday. This despite public and private pressure from many Republicans – aware they may lose the Senate in November – that he step aside now to give the president a chance to name a fourth member to the court. They say for now he enjoys the work, and feels he is able to serve with commitment and focus.

articles.title: Iran could move shadow war in a dangerous direction, experts warn on back of two possible terror attacks
articles.summary: Two suspected plots near RAF Fairford and aboard a FlyDubai flight raise questions about Iran's covert attacks against the United States and Israel.
articles.body: The FlyDubai stabbing is contributing to concerns that Iran could increase covert and deniable attacks as the conflict with the United States and Israel drags on. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, meanwhile, said there are "strong indications" Iran played a role in a suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford, the British air base used by U.S. forces during operations against Iran. Counterterrorism police have since arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. The two suspected attacks are raising questions over whether Iran's war strategy is shifting, but experts caution not to treat the incidents as equally indicative of Iranian involvement — or evidence yet that Tehran has changed its tactics. FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS President Donald Trump said early information he has received points to a possible Iranian connection to the attack aboard an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight, where a co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft with more than 180 people aboard. The United Arab Emirates and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have described the FlyDubai incident as terrorism, but UAE authorities have not publicly attributed the attack to Iran. Neither investigation has publicly established that the Iranian government directed the attacks, and Iran has denied involvement in the Fairford case. Daniel Byman, director of the Warfare, Irregular Threats and Terrorism Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Fairford case fits more closely with Iran's recent use of hired operatives and other intermediaries. "The attack on the airbase in the United Kingdom does fit more recent patterns," Byman told Fox News Digital, while stressing how much remains unknown about the investigation. RUBIO CONFIRMS 'FOREIGN ACTOR' INVOLVED IN UK TERROR PLOT The FlyDubai attack would be a more significant departure. "That is quite different, and that is something that Iran in the past, at least we haven't seen Iran do," Byman said. "It is plausible to me that Iran is involved, but that seems like much more of a stretch based on Iran's traditional way of operating." But the uncertainty surrounding the attacks also illustrates part of the appeal of the broader strategy Iran has spent decades developing: using proxies, covert operatives, criminal networks and other intermediaries to threaten adversaries far beyond its borders while making Tehran's own role more difficult to establish. Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury and FBI counterterrorism official who now directs the Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence at the Washington Institute, said Iran has increasingly sought to put more distance between itself and the people carrying out overseas operations. "Typically Iran does not admit that it's involved in these types of attacks because it wants reasonable deniability," Levitt said. "There are several advantages for Iran to using terrorism," Byman said. "One is that there is often a degree of deniability." "Terrorism gives Iran a lot more reach," he added. Levitt, however, put the distinction with conventional warfare more bluntly. "If Iran shoots a drone or a missile at you, you know where it came from and you know where to shoot back," he said. "But if Iran uses proxies, and recruits people and does things in a covert manner, it might not be so easy to point a finger back at Iran or to know exactly who did it." That capability matters in part because Iran does not have the conventional military strength to match the United States and its allies directly, Levitt said. "They just don't have the capability to fight soldier to soldier, airplane to airplane in an all-out kinetic war, but they're extremely effective at asymmetric warfare, at covert terrorist activity, if that's what this proves to be," he said. UK AIRBASE TERROR SUSPECTS BEING RELEASED ON BAIL AS IRAN DENIES CONNECTION Recent U.S. prosecutions have shown how far that playbook can extend. Federal cases have accused Iranian operatives of seeking to recruit hitmen to kill U.S. officials and using Eastern European organized crime figures in a murder-for-hire plot targeting Iranian-American journalist and dissident Masih Alinejad in New York. Those operations relied on the same basic advantage: Tehran could pursue targets overseas without launching a conventional attack that immediately identified Iran as the aggressor. The question now is whether the current conflict gives Iran reason to push that strategy further. Levitt said Tehran could pursue overseas plots in an effort to pressure Western governments to end the conflict by demonstrating that Iran can impose costs far beyond the conventional battlefield. And if Fairford and FlyDubai are ultimately tied to Tehran, he said, they would stand out because they involve harder targets and potentially more ambitious tactics than the assassinations, kidnappings, shootings and smaller-scale bombings Iran has more commonly pursued overseas. "Perhaps this is the new normal, and Iran wants to demonstrate that it can exact a higher cost," Levitt said. Byman, however, pointed to several reasons Tehran could exercise restraint. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Iran already has other ways to pressure Washington and its allies, while a terrorist attack against Americans could backfire by uniting U.S. public opinion behind further escalation against Tehran, he said. U.S. and Israeli strikes against senior Iranian intelligence and security officials may also have disrupted some of the networks Tehran would need for overseas operations. "If Iran wants to go further, then terrorism does become more of an option," Byman said.

articles.title: Trump says polls 'don't account for one thing,' as he pledges to defeat communists 'once and for all'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump told a cheering Dayton, Ohio, rally crowd that polls don't account for him campaigning as Republicans face a tough House path.
articles.body: President Donald Trump vowed that Republicans will overcome their disadvantage in the polls now that he is on the campaign trail on Saturday night. Trump held a rally in Dayton, Ohio, on Saturday and told a cheering crowd that the polls hadn't accounted for him campaigning personally. "On election night, Ohio is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it. America belongs to those who love it," Trump said. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS "These fake polls, they don't account for one thing. They don't account for the fact that Trump is out campaigning. They never thought this was good. They never thought this was going to happen," he added. A recent Fox News Poll found Democrats have a wider path to victory than Republicans in the House of Representatives. Democrats are projected to win 215 seats compared to 201 for the GOP, meaning the left only needs three more victories out of the 19 possible toss-up races to clinch a majority. Republicans would need to win at least 17 of those races. 10 DEMOCRAT-HELD HOUSE SEATS REPUBLICANS COULD FLIP TO SAVE THEIR MAJORITY "With you at my side, we have always prevailed and prevailed by a lot and got record-setting votes and record-setting victory," Trump said. "We've won every battle. We've defeated every hope. We've overcome every threat. And now we are on the cusp of beating the communists, socialist, radicalized lunatics and villains once and for all. We're going to put them down once and for all." A new memo being sent to Republicans across the country, first obtained by Fox News Digital, revealed four key topics that the House GOP is focusing on in the final four weeks before Election Day: the border, fraudulent use of taxpayer dollars, the economy and public safety. Republicans are also seeing political opportunity in the far-left insurgency that's gripped the Democratic Party during its primary cycle, warning that socialists are pushing the party further left than the majority of Americans. SOCIALISTS ARE HELPING GOP CAMPAIGNS HEADING INTO NOVEMBER The economy, including high grocery and gas prices, has become a central issue in the 2026 election cycle. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Democrats have seized on Americans' struggle with cost-of-living as a political cudgel against Republicans, particularly using Trump's tariffs on allies like Canada and his war in Iran as arguments against the GOP. Fox News' Elizabeth Elkind contributed to this report.

articles.title: Gonzalo Bernardos, economista: "Una parte de la izquierda ha perdido la cabeza"
articles.standfirst: El analista reflexiona sobre lo que considera una radicalización de las ideologías
articles.summary: El analista reflexiona sobre lo que considera una radicalización de las ideologías
articles.body: Gonzalo Bernardos, economista, ha analizado en sus redes sociales lo que considera una radicalización de determinas posturas políticas. "Una parte de la izquierda en todo el mundo ha perdido la cabeza y su ideología nativa y también una gran parte de su electorado", ha publicado en su cuenta personal de X, antes Twitter. El experto ha agregado que las posiciones siempre avanzan hacia los extremos: "En lugar de rectificar, se escora mucho más". El catalán ha reflexionado sobre esta situación citando un meme sobre la evolución de las tendencias políticas. En él, aparecen tres posiciones, la izquierda, el centro y la derecha. Las personas ubicadas en el centro y en la derecha no se mueven a medida que pasan los años, pero sí lo hace la tercera, que avanza mucho más hacia la izquierda. Al hacerlo, la posición de centro queda más desequilibrada y, posteriormente, a esta persona se le llama fanática. "Muy bien descrito", ha reaccionado Gonzalo Bernardos. El experto también ha analizado la encuesta de intención de voto en las futuras elecciones autonómicas en Cataluña, publicada este domingo por La Vanguardia. El PSC y Aliança Catalana serían las principales fuerzas políticas, con 30 escaños cada una. ERC sumaría 23, VOX 18 y Junts, 16. Destaca especialmente el crecimiento de Aliança Catalana, de dos a 30, y el descenso de Junts, de 35 a 16. Gonzalo Bernardos ha valorado con pesar la noticia: "Es una pena, pero es lo que hay. Después de más de diez años de nefasta gestión por parte de los diferentes Gobiernos de la Generalitat y en los últimos de hacer políticas de extrema izquierda (Aragonés e Illa), los catalanes han dicho basta. Votan a lo nuevo, a lo diferente y Aliança Catalana está un paso de ser la formación más votada. Votan a la derecha (75 versus 60 escaños) porque la izquierda, al dejar de ser socialdemócrata y convertirse en extrema, ha fracasado estrepitosamente".

articles.title: GOP rising star helped topple Trump-backed incumbent. Now he's caught leadership's eye
articles.summary: Mike Haridopolos is emerging as a behind-the-scenes force on the East Coast, helping secure billions for NASA and Kennedy Space Center's future.
articles.body: It’s June 2026 and the summer’s intense heat is slowly creeping across the East Coast. In Florida, a different kind of heat is threatening to burn Republicans — a firestorm of political backlash that could at best force the GOP to spend millions more in the midterms, and at worst cost the party what should be a safely red House seat. Rep. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., was one of the first to sound the alarm publicly about embattled Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., and the scandals that could have sandbagged his re-election chances. It’s an unusually bold move for a first-term congressman, particularly when the House GOP leadership and the White House were still publicly backing Mills. But Haridopolos’ plan was well-executed — and with the help of Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., Mills went down as one of only four Republican incumbents to lose a primary in the 2026 midterm cycle. Republican election watchers saw the loss with some relief, privately feeling better about their chances with former journalist Ryan Elijah, who Haridopolos recruited to run, against Democratic former NASA official Bale Dalton. And Haridopolos was there with Elijah both figuratively and literally. The former local news anchor said he was "right there in the front row" during the primary debate. REPUBLICANS MOVE TO OUST EMBATTLED FLORIDA GOP LAWMAKER IN BITTER PRIMARY FIGHT "Not only was he there, he was kind of like the spin room. He did a lot of the media interviews, and that was huge for us," Elijah told Fox News Digital. TRUMP'S SUPPORT DOESN'T SAVE SCANDAL-PLAGUED LAWMAKER IN PRIMARY Haridopolos told Fox News Digital, "I recognized that Cory Mills was absolutely going to lose a general election against a solid Democrat candidate. And so I went to the leadership and, of course, the president's team and said, ‘Look, we need to find a way for Mills to step aside.’" "Unfortunately, Mr. Mills was not willing to step aside. And so I let the leadership and the president know that I'd be helping someone else in the primary," he continued. "It was not the easiest thing to do, taking on a colleague. But… this is a team sport and all of us need to work together." WATCH: CORY MILLS BLASTS DOJ PROBE AS ‘POLITICAL OP' AHEAD OF FLORIDA PRIMARY "Team sport" is an analogy that the Florida Republican has used frequently, and one that he’s used to try and define his tenure in the House. It’s paid off for him so far, with Haridopolos forging close relationships with both House GOP leaders and his peers. "He’s a trusted ally and somebody you can count on. He delivers. You never have to worry about where he’s going to be," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., who has known Haridopolos for roughly two decades, told Fox News Digital. The two politicos first forged a relationship in their respective state houses. When Haridopolos said he would launch a campaign for Congress, Scalise said he told him, "I want to be your first check… I want to support you." And in his short time so far, he's already been entrusted to lead a House panel. Haridopolos is chair of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee’s space subcommittee, a fitting position for someone whose district is home to the Kennedy Space Center despite his junior status. The Florida freshman said space has long been a passion of his, dating back to his efforts as a state lawmaker to bring the shuttle program back to his backyard. NASA'S ARTEMIS FOLLOW-UP MISSION 'RIGHT AROUND THE CORNER' AFTER SUCCESSFUL LUNAR FLIGHT "So many people were concerned that we'd go back to the post-Apollo days, which are very detrimental to the economy of Central Florida. And so at that time, Rick Scott was governor… We decided that we needed to not just rely on NASA but start pushing for public-private partnerships," Haridopolos said. The U.S. has seen an unprecedented resurgence of success in space in the last two years, partly propelled by the public-private partnerships that Haridopolos is pushing. NASA completed its historic Artemis II mission just this year, sending four astronauts around the moon and back in the first such mission in decades. PETER NAVARRO: TRUMP'S ARTEMIS VISION IS NOW FLYING — AND CHINA IS PAYING ATTENTION "I'm really confident that in two years we'll be landing back on the moon," Haridopolos said. That’s also due in no small part to the federal government investing in the new space race, after the Trump administration initially proposed a roughly 24% cut to NASA’s budget in May 2025. Haridopolos, seeing space as another frontier for national security, was alarmed. He told Fox News Digital at the time that he would seek a "constructive conversation with the White House" about a higher figure. "I’m not sure what that number will be in the end, but in my conversations with the president about space, he’s absolutely committed to it," he said in May 2025. Eventually, President Donald Trump signed into law a spending bill that included $24.4 billion for NASA — rather than the initial $18.8 billion proposal — and approved an additional $9.9 billion in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox News Digital that Haridopolos "understands that so much of America’s future in space runs through Florida and Kennedy Space Center." "He is serious about the mission, willing to engage on the hard issues, and always focused on how we can move the ball forward," Isaacman said. Before his political career began, Haridopolos was a history professor at what is now Eastern Florida State College. He was born to an American mother and Greek immigrant father, and is currently married to Stephanie Haridopolos — a physician by profession who has spent the last several months as acting surgeon general. But despite his accomplishments and connections, Haridopolos’ name is not one that has garnered headlines in the way that more bombastic House Republicans have in their public defiance of GOP leaders or criticism of Trump. That’s because he prefers to settle disputes behind closed doors, a hallmark of politics that has largely been abandoned in an age where attention is seen as political currency. "When you hear members of Congress saying, like, ‘Oh, I want you to get me on TV,’ it's usually like, ‘Uh-oh, someone’s about to do something crazy here to get on TV.’ He was like… I’m going to earn my spot on there legitimately by being a good, reliable messenger for the party," a Republican aide familiar with Haridopolos’ operation told Fox News Digital. The aide said that could pose a challenge in times when television networks were looking for dramatic tales of discord, but that his communication skills still got him a "high volume" of press. That aide said they also witnessed Haridopolos turn down media interviews that did not fit his schedule, but offer to help fellow House Republicans secure that spot instead. "He was just finding ways to help out leadership, but also just his fellow members, especially his fellow freshman members," the aide said. Haridopolos told Fox News Digital of the chaos that’s become a regular facet of Republicans' majority, "One of my goals is to tell those folks who always stand [in front of cameras] after we finish the session, you know, what we need to do more is spend time in the caucus having these knock-down, drag-outs. Not through the press, but as a family, and come out there unified. I think it's the best way to solve problems." He’s also been known to offer help on the fundraising side — as Scalise put it, "He raises a lot of money." The political maneuvering has raised questions for some about where Haridopolos sees his future and what he’s looking to get out of the relationships he is building in a largely transactional world. "He knows how to work with people and how to advance what he wants," the Republican aide said. "I could see him in senior leadership… and sooner than people expect." Scalise said, "Mike has a bright future, because he's a natural leader." But Haridopolos has insisted that his efforts are all dedicated to the greater good of the Republican Party. "A lot of people have asked me if I'm going to pursue a leadership position after the elections this year. I'm absolutely not going to pursue one of those leadership positions," he said. "There's people who have been in Congress for three, four, or five terms who I think have really put that effort in." He named members like fellow freshman Rep. Brian Jack, R-Ga., Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, and Rep. Rudy Yakym, R-Ind. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If I'm focused on the team, I think great things could happen in the future," Haridopolos said.

articles.title: Trump launching 'Super Intelligence Force' to ensure American dominance
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said his new "Super Intelligence Force" will engage tech companies, religious groups and infrastructure providers to lead in superintelligence.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced Sunday the creation of a new federal "Super Intelligence Force" tasked with coordinating the government’s efforts to keep the United States at the forefront of rapidly developing artificial intelligence technology. The new force, known as SIF, will coordinate federal engagement with consumers, public-interest and religious groups, critical infrastructure providers and technology companies, Trump said in a Truth Social post. "The Super Intelligence Force is tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump wrote. TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS Trump said the technology "is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet" and would "protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." The president said the effort will be led by senior administration officials and report directly to him and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. TRUMP REBRANDS AI, REJECTS 'GLOBALIST SCHEME' TO CONTROL TECH Last week, Trump officially renamed artificial intelligence to "Super Intelligence" across the executive branch, following a high-level summit with top tech leaders at the White House. Trump, who has opposed imposing formal guardrails on SI, said at the time that the tech executives signed a "morally binding" document he dubbed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. "They almost viewed it as a separate kind of constitution," Trump said of the tech leaders. "When they signed that, it meant a lot." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X later that day that he viewed the summit as a "positive step." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think it's a significant positive step that the leaders of every major American lab have committed to implementing robust internal controls and multiple layers of audits and reviews," Zuckerberg wrote. Fox Business' Sophia Compton contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dems hand GOP fresh midterm weapon by opposing widely used voter ID
articles.summary: Senate Democrats blocked a voter ID and insider trading ban bill as Republicans like Chuck Schumer's caucus face accusations of denying Trump a win.
articles.body: Senate Democrats’ recent rejection of voter ID is giving Republicans fresh ammunition in the midterm fight, putting them on the opposite side of a practice that is common across the country and broadly popular with voters in both parties. Republicans have developed a cynical view of why Democrats won’t play ball with voter ID, arguing that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus don’t want to give the GOP a win heading into the midterm elections. "Democrats are gonna vote against it because they don't want to give the president a win," Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital. "They don’t want to give Republicans a win. They'll screw the country and stuff." DOZENS OF HOUSE DEMOCRATS REJECT BILL FUSING CONGRESSIONAL STOCK BAN WITH FEDERAL VOTER ID Republicans' latest attempt to pass a federal voter ID law, which was paired with another popular issue to ban insider trading in Congress, comes months after initially launching their push to pass the SAVE America Act, a high priority for President Donald Trump that Schumer and Democrats have time and again rejected. Earlier this year, Democrats argued that voter ID isn’t so bad, it’s just how Republicans were approaching it that they disagreed with — Schumer dubbed the SAVE America Act "Jim Crow 2.0" and contended it would disenfranchise Black and Brown voters. "Democrats support voter ID," Schumer said on a press call earlier this year. "In fact, we included it, and it is included, in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago." INSIDE THE SENATE'S CHAOTIC ALL-NIGHTER THAT LEFT TRUMP'S SAVE AMERICA ACT ON THE SHELF But as the months have dragged on, an issue that voters overwhelmingly support has become a place for Democrats to dig their heels into the dirt against. Requiring identification to vote is already a practice in 36 states. Of those, 23 require photo ID, while 13 accept another form of identification, such as a bank statement. Nine of those states have Democratic senators. "We already have it," Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told Fox News Digital. "I mean, Virginia has a voter ID law that our citizens really like." "Virtually every state has a voter ID law," he continued. "So, what, there has to be a one size fits all federal thing for states [that[ are already doing this?" SCHUMER, DEMOCRATS SAY THEY SUPPORT VOTER ID, THEN BLOCK GOP AMENDMENT TO REQUIRE IT Republicans say that the Democratic resistance has a more nefarious intent. Requiring voter ID would allegedly nuke some of their voter base, illegal immigrants, and therefore lower their chances of winning in federal elections. "Well, it's evident Democrats want to make it easier to cheat," Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Fox News Digital. " Republicans want to make it easier to vote, make sure nobody's cheating. And that's where we are on this voter ID, an 80/20 issue or not even more." Barrasso argued that identification is required in several mundane instances of life, from boarding a plane to buying a beer — and even to get into some rallies held by Democratic candidates during this election cycle. "But [what] we need to do is elect more Republicans to be able to win these elections and make sure we have people here that see what the American people see, which is, you have to have a photo ID to vote."

articles.title: WATCH: Dem senators dodge backing Kamala Harris in potential 2028 run: ‘Very messy’
articles.summary: Democratic senators aren't rallying behind Kamala Harris despite her frontrunner status, with a wide open primary looming for the 2028 race.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris is leaving the door open to another White House bid in 2028, but Democratic senators aren’t rushing to line up behind their party’s 2024 nominee. "Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support." "I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be." HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026 "We've got a lot of people who are going to run and I think we should sort that out after the midterms," Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., said. Harris returned to the campaign trail last week alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, while continuing to leave open the possibility of another White House bid. Asked in Detroit whether she would run in 2028, Harris said she had not decided and urged Democrats to focus on November, warning that "'28 won't matter" without success in 2026. "We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're gonna win back the House and the Senate." She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26." DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028 "This is going to be a wide open primary, and again, that's democracy at its best," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said. "Everyone who wants to run should be able to run for office here." Another potential 2028 contender is Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who represents the party’s progressive wing. Ocasio-Cortez describes herself as a democratic socialist. NEWSOM ROASTED ONLINE FOR 'STAGED' FLY-FISHING INTERVIEW WITH CNN ANCHOR WHERE HE DROPPED MAJOR 2028 HINT California Gov. Gavin Newsom is another potential 2028 contender, although he said last month that he would not run if Harris enters the race. "We should have a lot of candidates running so we have a very broad discussion about the future of this country," Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., said. Harris registered 5%. Neither Harris nor Ocasio-Cortez has announced a 2028 campaign.

articles.summary: RJD names Kunwar Rai for Darbhanga teacher seat, escalating rift with Congress; direct contests in 5 of 8 Bihar council seats ahead of Oct 23 polls.
articles.body: Patna: The differences between the RJD and Congress over their respective stakes in the elections to eight legislative council seats in the state escalated on Sunday with the RJD announcing party functionary Kunwar Rai as its candidate for the Darbhanga teacher constituency, represented by Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha.With the latest development, the RJD and Congress are now set for direct contests in five of the eight legislative council seats.Earlier, the RJD had fielded candidates for six seats while leaving the Darbhanga teacher constituency for the Congress and the Tirhut teacher constituency for the CPI. With Rai now in the fray, the RJD is contesting seven of the eight council seats going to polls on Oct 23.The move is significant for the Congress as Jha is a former state Congress chief and the lone Congress MLC left in the legislative council.“Our party selected Rai for the Darbhanga teacher constituency after due deliberation for strategic reasons. The party’s national chief Lalu Prasad recommended his name on the advice of our working president Tejashwi Prasad Yadav,” former RJD spokesman Ejaj Ahmad told reporters, adding that party’s state chief Mangani Lal Mandal formally announced Rai’s name.“Rai has been the state president of the party’s teachers’ cell.
