articles.title: The NO FAKES Act is a no-brainer: Your identity belongs to you
articles.summary: No one should have to worry that their face or voice can be copied, manipulated or used to deceive others.
articles.body:
With each passing day, scams are getting scarier. Now assisted by artificial intelligence, scammers are posing a greater risk to Americans than ever before in history.

People lose billions of dollars per year to impostor scams — up nearly threefold since 2020. Even before AI use became ubiquitous, impersonation fraud was all too rampant. Today, it translates to millions of individual reports of scamming and stealing every single year, and AI is making cloning tools even more powerful.

Case in point: Arizona mother Jennifer DeStefano . In 2023, DeStefano answered a phone call and heard her 15-year-old daughter crying and begging for help. Suddenly, a man took over the call, claiming that he had kidnapped DeStefano’s daughter and demanding a $1 million ransom for her safe return before lowering the demand to $50,000.

Before paying the ransom, DeStefano discovered her daughter was safe. When she later testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee, she described recognizing her daughter’s cries and the way she spoke. The committee identified her as the victim of an AI deepfake kidnapping and extortion scam.

This was back in 2023. With rapidly advancing AI , this problem is getting worse. AI makes it easier to imitate the people we trust and harder to know whether the person on the other end of a phone call — or appearing in a video on our screen — is real. Now, voice and image duplication are even more advanced. All that a scammer needs to duplicate a voice is three seconds of audio .

And scams are only the tip of the iceberg. AI-powered digital duplicates called deepfakes are concerning because they don’t require explicit human permission, wading into individual privacy, personal security, corporate reputation and other realms. Shouldn’t people have rights against digital duplicates?

In 2024, following an AI study that received more than 10,000 public comments , the U.S. Copyright Office concluded that existing AI-related protections contain massive gaps, recommending that Congress enact a federal law protecting all individuals against the knowing distribution of unauthorized digital replicas. The Copyright Office specifically stated the AI threat transcends entertainment and politics to private citizens — virtually every part of society.

Creatives know the problem firsthand, and they are demanding a solution. From musicians to voice actors, professionals have grown increasingly concerned about generative AI stealing from them — stealing them — when they are simply trying to make a living. Whether it’s James Bond or a Disney movie, AI developers are openly stealing copyrighted art , and it is wrong.

Intellectual property protections are just common sense. It is an 80-20 issue, if not even more popular. That’s why The Alliance for Secure AI, which I advise, recently launched “ Creatives for Secure AI ,” rallying creative professionals to confront the AI question and protect their likenesses. People should have meaningful control over convincing copies of themselves.

Congress is starting to see it that way, too. The bipartisan NO FAKES Act would establish protections for everyday Americans regarding digital duplicates. It would essentially create a federal intellectual property right to defend individuals from unauthorized digital replicas of their voice and visual likeness, protecting their privacy and livelihood.

The underlying principle is simple: Your identity belongs to you . No one should have to worry that their face or voice can be copied, manipulated or used to deceive others. At a time when AI development is moving too fast for public policy to catch up, Americans deserve protections that match the technology of our time and the speed of its deployment.

There are multiple layers to the AI threat. How many stories like DeStefano’s remain unsurfaced? How many artists and entertainers and performers will see their hard-earned identities co-opted by AI replicas without permission? How many countless victims of AI-powered overreach never get the justice they deserve?

These are difficult questions to answer, but our leaders can start by legislating with common sense. The NO FAKES Act is one place to start, so we can see progress on an issue that affects Democrats, Republicans, and independents alike.

The NO FAKES Act unanimously passed the Senate Judiciary Committee and is currently awaiting a vote on the Senate floor, but congressional leadership has yet to put it up to a vote. Our leaders must allow Congress to do its job and bring the bill to the floor for a vote.

Deepfakes are getting better. Scams are getting worse. It’s time for humans to speak out against the steal — and for Congress to listen.

Nico Zviovich is an advisor for The Alliance for Secure AI, where he launched Creatives for Secure AI. He is also an award-winning film producer and the chief impact officer of MovieGoer, a film distribution and marketing company.

articles.title: Supreme Court opens new term with shaky Trump relationship
articles.summary: The Supreme Court justices return to the bench Monday for their new term, and their docket is already filling up with new confrontations on President Trump’s immigration agenda, among other major cases. The term begins at a moment when the court’s public approval stands near record lows and in the shadow of a fraught relationship between Trump…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court justices return to the bench Monday for their new term, and their docket is already filling up with new confrontations on President Trump’s immigration agenda, among other major cases.

The term begins at a moment when the court’s public approval stands near record lows and in the shadow of a fraught relationship between Trump and the justices — namely the conservatives he appointed to the bench who have at times ruled against him.

“They voted against me too often,” Trump told Time magazine in an interview last week, referencing Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me, too.”

It’s that mixed record that has fueled questions about how Trump’s agenda will fare this term at the Supreme Court, as lower court judges repeatedly block the president’s policies, prompting the disputes to continually reach the justices in a barrage.

In just the past week, the justices cranked up their docket by adding two major appeals brought by the administration concerning the president’s immigration agenda.

The court will review whether officials are giving enough due process before deporting migrants to third countries where they have no ties. They’ll also rule on the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy, which has fueled a tsunami of litigation in the lower courts. Decisions in both cases are expected by summer.

“Because of the vast number of illegal immigrants — particularly during the Biden administration, but for many years up until now — that just creates an incredible backlog of issues and concerns,” said Carrie Severino, president of the Judicial Crisis Network and a former law clerk to Justice Clarence Thomas. “Particularly as this president is trying to actually enforce the immigration laws.”

“So, immigration is definitely an issue,” she noted.

It leaves groups that have prolifically fought the president in court, like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), gearing up for another major year at the Supreme Court.

“Last term, OT25 [October Term 2025], was one of the ACLU’s busiest ever,” Cecilia Wang, the group’s national legal director, told reporters during a briefing call last week. “This term may top that.”

Left-leaning groups have remained optimistic in their chances before the conservative-majority court after last term produced a mixed outcome for the president.

The court delivered Trump major wins on executive control over independent agencies and immigration but also struck down his signature tariff policy , thwarted his efforts to restrict birthright citizenship and blocked him from immediately firing Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook.

Trump’s foes have also found relief in the justices’ recent emergency decisions that kept the president’s mail-in voting plan blocked ahead of the midterms.

It’s some of those decisions that have left the president reeling. Trump, in one recent social media post, called his nominees “merely a shell of their original selves.”

In an interview with CBS News set to air Sunday, Justice Samuel Alito brushed off any notion the justices have a political agenda and pointed out the bipartisan nature of court criticism.

“He has his own way of saying things,” Alito said of Trump. “But the criticism of the court, I mean, I want to be even-handed on this. The criticism of the court by [former] President Biden and justices by President Biden and his administration was very harsh. And President Trump has been very harsh.”

The public attacks didn’t stop the president from inviting Kavanaugh and Barrett to join him at the recent state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, however.

It’s not just Trump being critical. The Supreme Court’s public approval stands near record lows. A record-high 43 percent of Americans believe the court is too conservative, according to a Gallup poll conducted in early September. Just a little more than one-third of those surveyed said it was “just about right” ideologically, and 17 percent said it was too liberal.

Beyond the upcoming cases that directly implicate Trump’s agenda, some touch on political issues about which Trump’s base cares deeply.

The justices will hear challenges to an Arizona law that requires documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote, a policy Republicans want implemented nationwide for federal elections. They’ll also take up several religious liberty disputes and examine the constitutionality of state bans on semi-automatic weapons, specifically AR-15s.

“We have a more exciting docket than we often do at this point,” said Severino.

“At the beginning of the Supreme Court term, some terms you would look at the list of the cases they’ve accepted already, and say, ‘Oh, it’s going to be kind of a snoozer,’” she added.

ACLU is asking the Supreme Court to add more cases to its plate. Among its pending requests is one that seeks to declare as unconstitutional Texas’s law requiring public school classrooms to post the Ten Commandments. The justices are set to consider taking up the case at a closed-door meeting after Texas responds in writing this fall.

“Our fundamental civil rights and civil liberties are under unprecedented attacks from all quarters,” Wang told reporters. “And many of those fights are poised to potentially make it up to the Supreme Court this term.”

On Monday, the term is set to begin with a bang as the justices consider a blockbuster case involving the fossil fuel industry. The Supreme Court will decide if cities and groups can use state law to force companies to pay potentially billions in damages over accusations they contributed to climate change and misled the public.

The case took an unanticipated turn last week when the court announced Alito’s last-minute recusal. Alito had faced pressure to exit the case due to perceived conflicts of interest related to his stock holdings in the oil and gas sector, but he told Bloomberg that his recusal was “prudent” — not required.

It’s a big week for Alito for unrelated reasons. On Tuesday, he’s set to release his first authored book since joining the bench, titled, “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country.” His CBS News interview is at the beginning of a rare media tour to promote it.

“It’s part of the job that you’re going displease people by making decisions on controversial matters, because one side or the other is going to really dislike you,” Alito told the outlet.

articles.title: Alito on Trump’s praise of him, criticism of fellow justices: ‘I put all of that out of my mind’
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito said in a rare televised interview Sunday on Fox News that he tries not to pay too much attention to President Trump’s frequent praise of him — and recent criticism of some of his fellow justices on the bench. “I put all of that out of my mind. I trust…
articles.body:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito said in a rare televised interview Sunday on Fox News that he tries not to pay too much attention to President Trump’s frequent praise of him — and recent criticism of some of his fellow justices on the bench.

“I put all of that out of my mind. I trust that my colleagues put all of that out of their minds,” Alito told “Fox News Sunday” host Shannon Bream when asked about the president’s recent comments.

“But I am concerned about the escalation in public rhetoric in general and about the things that people in important positions say about the Supreme Court as a whole and about individual justices. I’m concerned about the long-term effect of that on the standing of the court,” he added. “And, of course, if the court does not ultimately retain a degree of trust among the American people, that will be very deleterious.”

The associate justice’s remarks come after Trump said in a Time magazine interview that he regrets nominating conservative Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

“What can I do? I put them in,” Trump said. “They voted against me too often.”

The president also railed against those justices — but not by name — after the high court blocked his mail voting plan . “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal,” the president wrote on Truth Social last month.

But in that same social media post, Trump praised Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas as “legends,” noting their dissent against the ruling. The president earlier this year also commended Alito for writing the court’s landmark decision to limit a central provision of the Voting Rights Act.

Alito’s comments about public rhetoric aimed at justices more broadly follow two of his fellow jurists, Barrett and Justice Elena Kagan, telling lawmakers in a July testimony that the court needs more money to defend against the persistent rise in threats targeting them and their families.

Alito told CBS News in another interview this week that he’d considered retiring from the Supreme Court at the end of its most recent term. He also said his vote to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022 alongside the court’s other conservative justices took “ courage .” On Sunday, Alito told Fox News he “wasn’t surprised” at the backlash to the ruling.

“I anticipated that it would anger a great many people who believed and continue to believe strongly that there should be a constitutional right to abortion. So I understood that,” he said. “I didn’t anticipate the particulars, what that would — the forms that that reaction would take, the most extreme forms.”

articles.title: Emanuel urges Democrats to prioritize ethics reform over potential third Trump impeachment
articles.summary: Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel (D) on Sunday pushed Democrats to focus on ethics reform instead of a third impeachment of President Trump if they win back power in Congress after the midterm elections. “I’m for the investigations. Hold this administration accountable, which is what the Republican Congress and Senate has refused to do, which…
articles.body:
Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel (D) on Sunday pushed Democrats to focus on ethics reform instead of a third impeachment of President Trump if they win back power in Congress after the midterm elections.

“I’m for the investigations. Hold this administration accountable, which is what the Republican Congress and Senate has refused to do, which is why rather than set up a wedding party in your registry at Williams Sonoma, this administration allows Donald Trump Jr. to allow the Kremlin to be where you register,” Emanuel told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press,” referencing a ProPublica report about a Russian oligarch funding the president’s son’s wedding celebration.

“They paid $170,000 for a wedding party. And nobody thought it was wrong. That tells you the sense of impunity that’s operating,” he added.

Emanuel, who was also former President Obama’s chief of staff during his first term, then pushed Democrats to “pass an ethics package.”

“You’re never going to get an impeachment. Then if you do that, you just basically proved all Washington is what the American people think,” he said.

Trump was impeached twice during his first term, but Democrats haven’t made much of an effort to impeach the president again during his second term, beyond a bid by Rep. Al Green (D-Texas), which was voted down by several House Democrats.

Democrats appear poised to recapture the House, with Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasting they’ll have 238 seats following this year’s midterms . The current electoral environment is also favorable for Democrats, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s poor approval rating and concerns about the economy dragging on the GOP.

According to DDHQ , Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 38.6 percent on Sunday afternoon, with his disapproval rating at 59.3 percent.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: Trump shares meme labeling Obama, not Nixon, as ‘most corrupt president’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday continued his pattern of blasting former President Obama, sharing a meme stating that he, not former President Nixon, was the country’s “most corrupt” president. Trump posted a split screen of Obama and Nixon’s presidential portraits to Truth Social, with the photo including the caption, “One of these men is the most…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday continued his pattern of blasting former President Obama, sharing a meme stating that he, not former President Nixon, was the country’s “most corrupt” president.

Trump posted a split screen of Obama and Nixon’s presidential portraits to Truth Social , with the photo including the caption, “One of these men is the most corrupt president in the history of the United States. The other is Richard Nixon.”

The incumbent president has long criticized Obama, his direct Democratic predecessor. Before running for president, Trump falsely claimed that Obama was born in Kenya and not Hawaii.

Obama has recently taken his successor to task regarding his opposition to regulating artificial intelligence companies and the Iran war, saying in June the U.S. was “ worse off ” than prior to the conflict.

“We’ve now fought a war, spent billions and billions of dollars, put an enormous strain on our military, a lot of people have died and it feels like we are back where we were before we started the war, except maybe a little worse off,” the former president told host Craig Melvin on NBC’s “ Today .”

Trump on Sunday compared Obama to Nixon, who resigned in August 1974 amid revelations of his knowledge of the break-in at the Democratic National Committee headquarters, known as the “Watergate” scandal.

Nixon is the only American president to resign from office, while the House has impeached three presidents: Andrew Johnson in 1868, Bill Clinton in 1998 and Trump himself twice, in 2019 and 2021 .

In all four instances, the Senate acquitted the sitting president. The upper chamber has never removed a president from office.
